title: Spacer-Mediated Gold Nanocube Arrays for Edge-Localized Excitonic Enhancement in Monolayer MoS2
authors: Abdullah Efe Yildiz, Emre Ozan Polat
abstract: Plasmonic nanostructures offer an effective route for enhancing light-matter interaction in atomically thin semiconductors, whose optical response is intrinsically limited by their sub-nanometer active thickness. Here, we numerically investigate excitonic enhancement in monolayer (ML) Molybdenum Disulfide (MoS2) coupled to size-tuned gold (Au) nanocube arrays separated by thin aluminum oxide (Al2O3) and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) spacer layers. By varying the nanocube side length, the localized surface plasmon resonance is tuned across the visible spectral range to modulate the A- and B-excitonic transitions of monolayer MoS2. We show that the nanocube-size-dependent spectral redshift can be further controlled through the spacer material and thickness, enabling systematic tuning of the near-field distribution, carrier generation rate, quantum yield, and radiative decay enhancement. Localized plasmonic confinement yields excitation-rate enhancements of up to 4.35 at B-excitonic transition (605 nm) and 3.66 at A-excitonic transition (650 nm), while the radiative decay-rate enhancement exceeds 80, leading to 350-fold photoluminescence enhancement. Although both A- and B-excitonic channels are enhanced simultaneously, their relative contributions depend on nanocube size, spacer material, and spacer thickness, indicating wavelength-dependent excitonic modulation rather than strict exciton-selective switching. These findings establish Au nanocube arrays as a simple, scalable, and tunable plasmonic platform for enhancing excitonic carrier generation and emission in ML MoS2.
summary: The research demonstrates that coupling monolayer MoS2 to tunable gold nanocube arrays creates a highly efficient plasmonic platform for enhancing excitonic emission. By controlling the size and spacer material between the AuNCs and MoS2, researchers can systematically tune the near-field enhancement, leading to substantial boosts in carrier generation rates and photoluminescence quantum yield.
main_problem: The primary challenge is enhancing light-matter interaction, specifically excitonic processes, in atomically thin semiconductors like monolayer MoS2 due to their intrinsic optical thickness limitations.
main_result: Au nanocube arrays serve as a simple, scalable, and tunable plasmonic platform capable of significantly enhancing both the carrier generation rate and photoluminescence (PL) emission in ML MoS2.
method: The study uses numerical simulations (FDTD method) to model the coupling between localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPR) from Au nanocubes and excitonic transitions in MoS2.
model_or_system: The system consists of monolayer MoS2 coupled to size-tuned gold nanocube arrays separated by tunable dielectric spacer layers, such as Al2O3 or h-BN. The coupling strength is modulated by the plasmon resonance tuning and the thickness/material of the spacer.
key_observables: Excitation-rate enhancement (up to 4.35 at B-exciton), radiative decay-rate enhancement (>80), photoluminescence enhancement ($\sim$350-fold), and the spectral dependence of these enhancements across A- and B-excitonic transitions.
important_parameters: Au nanocube side length, spacer material (Al2O3 vs h-BN), and spacer thickness ($t_s$).
main_assumptions: The enhancement mechanism is attributed to the combined effect of spectral overlap between LSPR and excitons, and distance-dependent near-field coupling; it is not strictly an exciton-selective switching process.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate plasmonic response (extinction spectra), in-plane electric field intensity ($	ext{|E|}^2$) dependence on spacer thickness, normalized absorption spectra showing retained excitonic features, and carrier generation rate/quantum yield vs. spacer thickness.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates the physical platform by first establishing the need for enhancement, then detailing how tuning AuNC size and spacer properties controls the LSPR, which in turn modulates the near-field coupling to enhance excitonic processes (CGR and PL).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum optics and open quantum systems concepts by modeling engineered light-matter interaction platforms. The quantitative enhancement factors provide concrete metrics for designing solid-state emitters.

Figure 4 presents the carrier generation rate of monolayer MoS2 coupled to periodic AuNC arrays. Unlike the normalized absorption spectra in Figure 3, the carrier generation rate gives a more direct measure of how efficiently incident light produces electron-hole pairs inside the MoS2 monolayer. Therefore, this analysis is useful for evaluating the practical effect of plasmonic near- field enhancement on excitonic light harvesting.
